faq.question: How does the floating teleprompter work?
faq.answer: CueCard opens a small window that stays on top of your other apps. Start the script scrolling, switch to the app you record in, and the window stays where you can read it. It is on your screen and not in front of the lens, so the camera never records it.

faq.question: Is CueCard available for iPhone and Android?
faq.answer: The iPhone and iPad app is out now on the App Store, and it is free. The Android app is still being built.

faq.question: Can I use it with my camera app?
faq.answer: Yes. CueCard floats over any app, including your phone's own camera, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and the rest.

faq.question: Is there a version for my computer?
faq.answer: Yes. CueCard for Mac and Windows keeps your speaker notes on your screen and out of your screen share on Zoom, Google Meet and Teams. It is a different app for a different job, and it is also free.

faq.question: Why is the floating window missing?
faq.answer: Return to CueCard and open the prompter with the green play button. Tap the script to reveal controls and look for Start Overlay. The overlay button appears when picture-in-picture is available. Close another active picture-in-picture window and try again. If it still fails, use the full-screen reader on a second device while recording.

faq.question: What if the script moves too fast?
faq.answer: Lower Scroll Speed in Settings and rehearse a short passage. Text size and window shape change how many words fit on each line, so check the pace again after resizing. Scrolling does not automatically follow your voice.

faq.question: What if CueCard covers a camera control?
faq.answer: Move the floating window to another corner. Adjust Dimension Ratio and Floating Prompter Text Size in CueCard Settings, then return to your recording app. Keep the recording and camera-switch buttons reachable.

faq.question: Will the script appear in my video?
faq.answer: Camera recording captures the image through the lens, so the floating script is not part of that footage. Phone screen recording or a screen broadcast can capture the window. Record a short camera test and review it before posting.

guide.heading: How to set up your mobile teleprompter
guide.intro: A saved script, a comfortable reading pace, and a window close to the lens are all you need to begin.

steps.title: Write and save your script
steps.body: Open CueCard and paste or type into the editor. The ellipsis menu includes New Note and Import from File. Choose Save as New to keep a named copy in your saved notes.

steps.title: Choose a readable size and pace
steps.body: Open Settings with the gear button. Set Scroll Speed in lines/min and Text Size under Floating Prompter. Choose a Dimension Ratio that leaves room for your camera controls. Scrolling runs at the speed you set; CueCard does not listen to your voice or track your speech.

steps.title: Start the floating window
steps.body: Return to the editor, hide the keyboard, and tap the green play button to open the prompter. Tap the picture-in-picture icon, labeled Start Overlay for accessibility. If the controls have faded, tap the script to show them. CueCard opens the floating window and minimizes. To use Start Delay for a fresh take, start playback in the full-screen prompter before opening the overlay.

steps.title: Open your camera and position the script
steps.body: Switch to the recording app and select its video camera. Move CueCard near the front-facing lens while keeping recording controls visible. On iPhone, start with a compact window and short lines to reduce sideways eye movement.

steps.title: Give yourself time to begin
steps.body: Set Start Delay in CueCard Settings before the take. Return to the full-screen prompter and restart, then press play to begin the countdown before opening the overlay. Floating-window play/pause controls scrolling; resuming plays immediately. The countdown controls the script, not your camera recording.

steps.title: Record, review, and adjust
steps.body: Record a short test take, then watch it back before posting. If your eyes sweep sideways, shorten the lines or narrow the window. If you sound rushed, lower Scroll Speed. Leave a beat at each [cue pause]; cue tags are colored reminders, not automatic pauses.

steps.title: Write and save your script
steps.body: Open CueCard and paste or type into the editor. The ellipsis menu includes New Note and Import from File. Choose Save as New to keep a named copy in your saved notes.

steps.title: Choose a readable size and pace
steps.body: Open Settings with the gear button. Set Scroll Speed in lines/min and Text Size under Floating Prompter. Choose a Dimension Ratio that leaves room for your camera controls. Scrolling runs at the speed you set; CueCard does not listen to your voice or track your speech.

steps.title: Start the floating window

steps.title: Open your recording app

steps.title: Keep the words near the lens
steps.body: Move the floating window close to the front camera without covering the record button or camera-switch control. Use short lines and text large enough to read without leaning toward the screen.

steps.title: Give yourself time to begin
steps.body: Set Start Delay in CueCard Settings before the take. Return to the full-screen prompter and restart, then press play to begin the countdown before opening the overlay. steps.title: Record, review, and adjust

steps.body: Return to the editor, hide the keyboard, and tap the green play button to open the prompter. Tap the picture-in-picture icon, labeled Start Overlay for accessibility. If the controls have faded, tap the script to show them. CueCard opens the floating window and minimizes. To use Start Delay for a fresh take, start playback in the full-screen prompter before opening the overlay.

steps.title: Open your recording app
steps.body: Rehearse the opening in your phone’s camera first. Then open your mobile camera broadcast setup in Twitch and arrange the floating window around the controls and chat. Screen broadcasts can capture the prompter, so use this workflow for a camera stream.

steps.title: Keep the words near the lens
steps.body: Move the floating window close to the front camera without covering the record button or camera-switch control. Use short lines and text large enough to read without leaning toward the screen.

steps.title: Give yourself time to begin
steps.body: Set Start Delay in CueCard Settings before the take. Return to the full-screen prompter and restart, then press play to begin the countdown before opening the overlay. Floating-window play/pause controls scrolling; resuming plays immediately. The countdown controls the script, not your camera recording.

steps.title: Record, review, and adjust
steps.body: Record a short test take, then watch it back before posting. If your eyes sweep sideways, shorten the lines or narrow the window. If you sound rushed, lower Scroll Speed. Leave a beat at each [cue pause]; cue tags are colored reminders, not automatic pauses.

[cue welcome]
Welcome in. Here is today’s plan.
First, a quick progress update.
Then I will show the next step.
[cue pause for chat]
Leave your questions and I will pick them up between sections.
